title: AI 2041: Ten Visions for Our Future
author: Kai-Fu Lee & Chen Qiufan
notes:
I listened to this as an audiobook AI 2041: Ten Visions for Our Future (2021). It was written in 2021 at the end of the Covid pandemic and just before ChatGPT was released, so a lifetime ago in terms of AI developments. However, the book is outstanding in its framing of real-world fictional scenarios and the discussion that follows.

AI 2041: Ten Visions for Our Future (2021) pairs Kai-Fu Lee (AI researcher, former president of Google China) with Chen Qiufan (acclaimed Chinese sci-fi novelist). The structure is unusual: each of the ten chapters opens with a short story set in 2041, written by Qiufan, depicting how a specific AI technology has reshaped daily life somewhere in the world — followed by a nonfiction essay from Lee that explains the real technology behind the story and forecasts how it's likely to develop over the next two decades. 

Each chapter pairs a story situated in 2041 by Chen Qiufan with an analytical essay by Kai-Fu Lee covering the present state of the technology and expectations for its development by 2041. The goal is to make abstract AI concepts (deep learning, GANs, quantum computing, AGI, etc.) tangible through narrative, while keeping the technical grounding rigorous. The book is generally optimistic about AI's potential to generate abundance, but doesn't shy away from risks like bias, job displacement, deepfakes, and autonomous weapons.

The Ten Visions, in Order

The Golden Elephant (India) — A deep-learning insurance/finance system makes decisions for a family that end up reinforcing caste and social biases, illustrating how data-driven optimization can entrench discrimination. Tech focus: deep learning, big data, AI bias/externalities.

Gods Behind the Masks (Nigeria) — A young programmer is pressured into producing a deepfake video meant to discredit a masked political movement, then has to find a way out of the scheme. Tech focus: computer vision, GANs, deepfakes, AI security.

Twin Sparrows (Seoul, South Korea) — Orphaned twin boys at an academy each design their own AI tutor/companion; one thrives under a gamified AI coach while the other (on the autism spectrum) flourishes with a gentler, creative AI guide — raising questions about over-optimized, achievement-obsessed parenting. Tech focus: natural language processing, GPT-style models, AI in education.

Contactless Love (Shanghai) — In a world still shaped by recurring COVID variants, a woman traumatized by the pandemic relies on robotic caregiving to manage daily life while struggling to reconnect with other humans. Tech focus: AI healthcare, robotics, pandemic-driven automation.

My Haunting Idol (Tokyo) — A devoted fan immerses himself in a virtual/AR recreation of a celebrity idol, exploring the seductive and potentially unhealthy pull of synthetic intimacy. Tech focus: VR/AR/mixed reality, brain-computer interfaces.

The Holy Driver (Munich) — Full vehicle autonomy collides with human trust, religion, and the role of people as mere "backups" to self-driving systems. Tech focus: autonomous vehicles, smart cities, ethics of automation.

Quantum Genocide (Munich/global) — A rogue quantum computing scientist plots revenge by threatening to break global encryption (including Bitcoin), nearly triggering catastrophe. Tech focus: quantum computing, cryptographic security, autonomous weapons/existential risk.

The Job Savior (San Francisco) — As automation displaces workers, a new "job reallocation" industry emerges to help people retrain and find new purpose. Tech focus: AI-driven job displacement, universal basic income debates.

Isle of Happiness — A society attempts to algorithmically measure and optimize human happiness itself, prompting philosophical questions about whether fulfillment can—or should—be quantified. Tech focus: AI and wellbeing metrics, the limits of optimization.

Dreaming of Plenitude (Mumbai) — A closing, more utopian vision of a post-scarcity world, where AI-optimized renewable energy (solar, wind, storage) drives costs toward zero and reshapes manufacturing and poverty itself. Tech focus: post-scarcity economics, clean energy + AI synergy.

A useful framing: the book moves roughly from individual/social harms (bias, deepfakes, education pressure) through technological risk (autonomy, quantum threats) to economic disruption and, finally, a more hopeful long-term vision — ending deliberately on abundance rather than dystopia.

title: A Giant Leap
author: Robert M. Wachter
notes:
Just read Robert Wachter's A Giant Leap, an accessible, well-written, and clinically grounded primer — arguably the best single-volume introduction to AI in healthcare available today. Wachter, an academic hospitalist chair of medicine at UCSF, is a serious thinker, not a naive booster, and his awareness of past digital disappointments (his previous book, The Digital Doctor, was a warning about EHRs) gives his cautious optimism some credibility.
But the book ultimately reflects the view from the top of American academic medicine — optimistic, well-funded, and influential, but not representative of where most care actually happens. Readers should treat it as an essential starting point, not a verdict.

I found the book to be a refreshing read documenting the many failed attempts at "AI in healthcare" spanning many decades where the initial failed attempts were overly ambitious (i.e. focusing on the most complex tasks such as diagnosis and interpretation). He reviews the gradual transition from paper charts to electronic medical records (EHR) in the early 2000s, with the unintended consequence of tasking clinicians with manually typing out their daily notes (keeping them glued to the screen) and frustrating them with administrative burden including managing an in box from patients and fighting insurers for prior authorization requests. The book thankfully transitions to the past 5 years with the introduction of generative AI, being rapidly applied to some of these basic tasks (i.e. new software that captures a routine doctor-patient visit into a standard chart note referred to as "AI scribe" or "ambient AI"), far exceeding all prior attempts (i.e. dictation transcription, human scribes, templates). Generative AI is being used to summarize large patient volumes with great accuracy. In addition, he notes niche applications where AI is starting to process large volumes of data to provide innovative applications (i.e. take a standard EKG and accurately provide a cardiac ejection fraction!).

Wachter does a great job introducing (name dropping?) a variety of startups fiercely competing in this AI healthcare scribe space (Abridge, Epic-MS partnership, Oracle/Cerner), or the prior auth space (Ochsner Health opening its EHR to an insurer, or Elevance/Anthem connecting with Montefiore's Epic EHR). He gushes over the concept of a doctor "digital twin" being embraced at the Mayo Clinic or the AI medical student application screening tool being used at NYU Langone! 

One highly interesting section discussed the inability of large private companies to crack the primary care model in the US. These include failures at Amazon's One Medical, CVS's Oak Street Health, Walgreen's VillageMD, and start-ups Google's Forward, UK's Babylon Health, and now Cure Ai. The bet is whether private tech enterprise will figure it out or much more likely established health systems will dominate and integrate AI.

Critical Weaknesses

1. Optimism bias is structural, not incidental.

Wachter's position — an elite academic physician at a flagship institution with deep ties to the tech-medicine world — shapes his perspective in ways the book does not fully interrogate. His 100+ interviews are largely with "pioneers," which almost by definition skews toward boosters. Skeptics, frontline nurses, community health workers, and underserved patients are not the architects of his narrative.

2. The "better than broken" standard is dangerously low.
His central argument — AI just needs to beat a dysfunctional status quo — could be used to justify deploying undertested tools on vulnerable populations. A system causing a million annual harms is not a neutral baseline. This framing risks accelerating AI adoption before rigorous outcome data exists across diverse patient populations.

3. Algorithmic risks are acknowledged but not sufficiently weighted.
Wachter acknowledges algorithmic drift — where AI performance degrades over time as science, policies, or patient populations change — but treats it as a manageable concern rather than a systemic risk. The structural conditions under which AI fails (in under-resourced hospitals, in populations underrepresented in training data) receive far less attention than its successes at elite institutions. 

4. The equity problem is underexplored.
The book largely reflects the experience of well-resourced health systems. The AI tools Wachter describes are, for now, predominantly being piloted at places like UCSF and Mayo Clinic. What happens when stripped-down versions reach safety-net hospitals or rural clinics is largely unaddressed — a major gap given that healthcare inequality is arguably the system's deepest failure.

5. It risks aging poorly, fast.
The book's insertion of AI into healthcare is set against a backdrop of eroding trust between patients and clinicians, and a political landscape where partisanship has infected patients' perceptions of clinical recommendations — dynamics Wachter notes but doesn't fully integrate into his optimistic arc. In a field moving as fast as this one, a framework built in 2025â2026 may need significant revision within 2â3 years. 

6. The blurb problem.
The endorsements — from Marc Benioff (Salesforce CEO), Vinod Khosla (AI investor), and Microsoft Research's president — signal that this book is embedded in the same tech-medicine industrial complex it is meant to evaluate. These aren't neutral validators.

I highly recommend this book to anyone in healthcare and anyone who has interest in how AI is changing our world.

Key Reference:

Screening for Cardiac Contractile Dysfunction Using an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Electrocardiogram.
Nature Medicine. 2019. Attia ZI, Kapa S, Lopez-Jimenez F, et al.

title: The Vigil
author: George Saunders
notes:
Just listened to the audiobook “The Vigil” by George Saunders, the story is set around a man lying on his deathbed. As he drifts in and out of consciousness, he becomes aware of strange, otherworldly figures—angels or spirit-like beings—who gather around him. 

The dying man is K. J. Boone, an enormously wealthy oil tycoon / industrialist lying unconscious with cancer, and he is strikingly unrepentant about the damage he caused. The novel’s supernatural watchers are not really comforting, saintly angels so much as spirits or afterlife functionaries gathered around his deathbed. The central spirit is Jill Blaine, whose task is to guide Boone toward some recognition of guilt or moral clarity before death, but she finds that he has essentially no remorse: he remains convinced of his own importance and justification. Another spirit, including a hostile French engineer figure, presses the case against him more harshly, so the book becomes less a redemption story than a moral reckoning over wealth, extraction, climate harm, and whether a man who helped wreck the world can face judgment without ever truly admitting wrong.  

Tone of “The Vigil” (by George Saunders):
It’s darkly comic, satirical, and morally unsettling. Saunders blends absurd humor (the bickering, imperfect “angels” or spirits) with a bleak ethical core—a powerful man facing death without remorse. The tone oscillates between grotesque comedy and quiet dread, never offering clean redemption. There’s also a strong undercurrent of moral irony: the cosmic system meant to judge or guide him feels as flawed as the man himself. Overall, it leaves you with discomfort rather than catharsis.

I didn’t love the book.

title: Bubble in the Sun
author: Christopher Knowlton
notes:
Just read Chris Knowlton's Bubble in the Sun: The Florida Boom of the 1920s and How It Brought on the Great Depression (2020).  This is a captivating history of the aggressive development of the east coast of Florida by wealthy industrialists and the go-go culture of the roaring 1920s with a great migration of people to make a buck in real estate. 

The story focuses on 4 men and a woman. Henry Flagler, co-founder of Standard Oil (along with JD Rockefeller) takes his wealth to St Augustine and begins an ambitious second career building mega hotel resorts and importantly the Florida East Coast Railway, which connects the east coast to Miami initially, then extends to the keys!  Other notable characters include Carl Fisher who made his fortune in the auto industry develops the local roads around Miami, George Merrick has a vision for a new city in Coral Gables, and Addison Mizner (along with his dead-beat brother Wilson) who is a creative architect who develops Boca and Palm Beach with massive resort hotels and private residences. Marjorie Stoneman Douglas is the daughter of the editor of Miami Herald, is a writer and environmentalist who focuses on preserving the Everglades (who lives to be 107 and was awarded the Presidential Medal by Obama at age 103).

The story focuses on greed and over exuberance on borrowing, debt-financed real estate deals, insider dealing by hucksters, lack of banking regulations leading to the collapse of Florida banks, preceding the stock market crash of 1929 and the protracted depression. All 4 luminaries reach great heights, before becoming penniless and dying prematurely!  The story is riveting and is probably less well-known than the westward migration, the gold rush (SF or Alaska), or Vegas!  There are elements of excess, greed, corruption, invincibility of the pioneering spirit.

https://www.amazon.com/Bubble-Sun-Florida-Brought-Depression/dp/1982128372

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
author: Douglas Adams
notes:
Just listened to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, by Douglas Adams (1979, the first book of a series).  I see this book being referenced often as dystopian. I first came across it in the Elon Musk biography by Walter Isaacson (apparently this was very influential on Musk!).  

The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is a sci-fi comedy that treats the universe as vast, absurd, and deeply indifferent—then laughs at it anyway.  Initially was a BBC Radio series that was adapted to many formats with a cult following.

The story begins when Arthur Dent, an utterly ordinary Englishman, discovers that Earth is about to be demolished to make way for an interstellar hyperspace bypass. He’s saved at the last second by Ford Prefect, who turns out not to be from Guildford but an alien researcher for a galactic travel book called The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy (whose most important advice is: “Don’t Panic.”)

As Earth is vaporized, Arthur is swept into space and joins a cast of gloriously dysfunctional characters:

Zaphod Beeblebrox, a two-headed, semi-insane galactic president

Trillian, a human who left Earth earlier and actually adapted

Marvin, a robot with a brain the size of a planet and crippling depression

They travel aboard the Heart of Gold, a spaceship powered by the Infinite Improbability Drive, which allows literally anything—however unlikely—to happen.

Along the way, the novel skewers bureaucracy, technology, philosophy, and humanity’s need for meaning. The book’s most famous revelation—that the Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything is 42—perfectly captures Adams’s core joke: the universe may have answers, but they’re useless without the right questions.

What it’s really about

The absurdity of existence

The futility (and comedy) of seeking cosmic meaning

Satire of politics, science, religion, and human self-importance

Why towels are the most important item you can carry

Tone

Fast, irreverent, philosophical, British, and relentlessly funny—less about plot than about ideas and punchlines that sneak up on you.

title: The Thinking Machine
author: Stephen Witt
notes:
Just listened to this outstanding book on the development of AI (and Nvidia as its core).  I found this book to be a bit "inside baseball" and quite technical but riveting as it explores most of the central actors in detail.

The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip is a narrative-driven biography + business history that explains how a relatively obscure graphics-chip company became one of the most powerful forces in artificial intelligence. The author, Stephen Witt, is an investigative journalist who gained extensive access to Nvidia’s leaders and insides of the company’s growth. 

ð§  Central Story

Jensen Huang’s life and leadership: The book traces Huang’s journey from his early life (sent to the U.S. as a child and facing hardship) to co-founding Nvidia and leading it for decades. 
Shortform

Pivot to AI computing: Nvidia originally made GPUs for video games, but Huang’s contrarian bet on parallel computing (doing many calculations simultaneously) positioned the company perfectly for the AI revolution, when researchers discovered GPUs could accelerate training large neural networks.

1. GeForce 256 (1999) — The First “GPU”

Innovation: Hardware transform & lighting (T&L)
Why it mattered:

Coined the term GPU (graphics processing unit).

Moved 3D math from the CPU to a massively parallel chip.

Introduced the core idea: many small cores > one big core.

ð Witt’s point: This wasn’t about games—it was the philosophical birth of parallel computing.

2. Programmable Shaders (Early 2000s) — Graphics Becomes Computation

Innovation: Programmable pixel & vertex shaders
Why it mattered:

Developers could write custom math programs on GPUs.

Scientists began using GPUs for non-graphics math (the earliest “GPGPU”).

ð Key transition: GPUs stop being fixed-function hardware and become flexible computing engines.

3. CUDA (2006) — The Masterstroke

Innovation: CUDA software platform (C/C++ for GPUs)
Why it mattered:

Turned GPUs into general-purpose supercomputers.

Locked developers into NVIDIA’s ecosystem years before AI exploded.

Enabled universities, labs, and startups to build GPU-native software.

ð Witt is explicit: CUDA—not silicon—was NVIDIA’s biggest moat.

4. Tesla GPUs (2007â2015) — Data Center Entry

Innovation: GPUs designed for scientific & enterprise workloads
Why it mattered:

GPUs moved into supercomputers, weather models, genomics.

NVIDIA became infrastructure, not a consumer gadget company.

ð Hidden win: NVIDIA learned how to sell to governments and hyperscalers long before rivals.

5. Deep Learning Breakthrough (2012) — Accidental Destiny

Innovation: GPUs used to train neural networks (AlexNet)
Why it mattered:

GPUs proved orders of magnitude faster than CPUs for neural nets.

NVIDIA became indispensable to AI research overnight—by luck, preparation, and CUDA.

ð Witt’s framing: AI didn’t choose NVIDIA—NVIDIA was already there.

6. Volta Architecture + Tensor Cores (2017) — AI-Native Hardware

Innovation: Tensor Cores (matrix math acceleration)
Why it mattered:

First chips explicitly designed for AI, not adapted later.

Massive speedups for training deep neural networks.

ð This is where NVIDIA stops riding AI and starts steering it.

7. A100 (Ampere, 2020) — The AI Workhorse

Innovation:

Multi-instance GPU (MIG)

Mixed-precision AI math
Why it mattered:

Became the default chip for training large language models.

Powered early ChatGPT-era systems.

ð Economic shift: NVIDIA hardware becomes the rate-limiting step of AI progress.

8. H100 (Hopper, 2022â2023) — AI Bottleneck Chip

Innovation:

Transformer Engine (LLM-optimized)

Extreme bandwidth & interconnects
Why it mattered:

Purpose-built for transformers (LLMs).

Global shortage â NVIDIA gains enormous pricing power.

ð Witt calls this the moment NVIDIA became geopolitically relevant.

9. NVLink & DGX Systems — Systems, Not Chips

Innovation:

High-speed GPU-to-GPU interconnects

Pre-assembled AI supercomputers
Why it mattered:

NVIDIA sells entire AI factories, not components.

Competitors struggle because integration is as important as silicon.

10. Grace Hopper Superchip (2023â) — CPU + GPU Fusion

Innovation:

NVIDIA-designed CPU tightly coupled to GPU
Why it mattered:

Reduced dependence on Intel/AMD CPUs.

Optimized for massive AI workloads and memory sharing.

ð Strategic shift: NVIDIA controls the full compute stack.

11. Software Stack (Ongoing) — The Real Lock-In

Innovation:

cuDNN, TensorRT, Triton, AI Enterprise
Why it mattered:

Hardware competitors can copy chips—but not decades of software tooling.

Developers build once, stay forever.

ð Witt’s verdict: NVIDIA is closer to Microsoft in the 1990s than Intel in the 2000s.

One-Line Synthesis (Very Witt-like)

NVIDIA didn’t win because it made faster chips—it won because it redefined what a computer is, then built the software, hardware, and culture to defend that definition for 20 years.

title: Breakneck: China's Quest to Engineer the Future
author: Dan Wang
notes:
Just read this fascinating book (quick read) that offers an interesting framework on the China - US dichotomy.

Wang claims that because China’s leadership and technocratic elite are engineers, decisions tilt toward construction and rapid execution. In contrast, U.S. policymakers trained in law elevate deliberation, compliance, and procedural checks, which slows action. China’s massive infrastructure and manufacturing capabilities aren’t incidental — they are instruments of national power. Wang shows how building capacity (e.g., EVs, semiconductor supply chains, nationwide rail) translates into geopolitical leverage. The same engineering mindset that builds megacities also tries to engineer people — resulting in harsh social policies, intense surveillance, and political repression. Wang doesn’t romanticize China; he highlights these trade-offs.  

Portrayal of the U.S. as merely “lawyerly” lacks depth and nuance compared to the richly detailed depiction of China’s engineering state. The American side risks caricature. The emphasis on legal caution can be reframed: protecting individual rights, environmental standards, and democratic accountability isn’t simply obstruction — it’s a foundation for sustainable and equitable societies that the “engineer state” approach too often sacrifices.

This book offers U.S.âChina competition beyond military confrontation — focusing on industrial policy, technology, and governance models. It challenges conventional dichotomies like capitalism vs. socialism or democracy vs. authoritarianism, offering functional lenses instead. Importantly, it encourages policymakers and business leaders to rethink institutional incentives shaping growth and innovation.

I highly recommend it.  

https://www.amazon.com/Breakneck-Chinas-Quest-Engineer-Future/dp/B0FDH3Z3K6/ref=sr_1_1?adgrpid=1343605749925404&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.de450CGFS5g8Uw

title: The Memoirs of Stockholm Sven
author: Nathaniel Ian Miller
notes:
Our local Collingswood Library Book Club featured Stockholm Sven by Nathanial Ian Miller as the monthly book.  I read this book and loved it!
It is set between 1910 and 1945 in the archipelago Spitsbergen near the arctic circle (off the Baltic coast from Sweden) featuring the memoir of an awkward man who leaves Stockholm for adventures and meets up with heart-warming characters for a harsh life.  The prose is thoughtful. There are no heroes, just survivors.

title: Notes on Being a Man
author: Scott Galloway
notes:
I just completed an audiobook that I wish to strongly endorse!  This is especially true for anyone with kids, boys in particular!  Galloway is a 60+ year old NYU business school prof who made money being a serial entrepreneur (sold L2, Inc, a marketing communications firm in 2017 for $130M) and is a skilled public speaker with podcasts, etc. 

Scott Galloway’s Notes on Being a Man is a sharp, candid, and often vulnerable reflection on what modern masculinity should look like—and what happens when men fail to evolve. Drawing from his own life story—growing up with financial insecurity, navigating ambition, failures, divorce, parenting, aging, and professional reinvention—Galloway offers a blend of memoir, social commentary, and tough-love guidance.

At the heart of the book is the thesis that traditional models of masculinity are obsolete, and that many men today suffer from loneliness, lack of purpose, and poor emotional skills. Galloway argues that being a good man is less about dominance, stoicism, or material success, and more about responsibility, emotional openness, discipline, and connection.

He explores themes such as:

The danger of isolation, especially among young men who lack mentors or meaningful relationships.

The importance of competence and resilience, not as performance, but as tools to support others.

Ambition and humility, and the paradox that real confidence comes from acknowledging your weaknesses.

Love and partnership, where he stresses loyalty, communication, and showing up consistently.

Fatherhood, and how being a present, emotionally intelligent parent is one of the highest callings of manhood.

Aging and mortality, including letting go of ego, accepting limitations, and shifting from “warrior” to “sage.”

Throughout, Galloway mixes harsh truths with humor and autobiographical honesty—admitting his own mistakes in relationships, work, and self-image. His overarching message: Manhood should be earned, not inherited, and it requires continuous growth, self-awareness, and service to others.

The book ultimately serves as both a critique of outdated masculine norms and a blueprint for healthier, more grounded male identity in the 21st century.

Here is a book review in the WSJ:

author: Andrew Ross Sorkin
notes:
Just read this chilling and instructive book by Andrew Ross Sorkin about the 1929 market crash.  Book focused on the period between 1928 - 1934, at the end of the "roaring 1920s".

Sorkin emphasizes people, incentives and personality rather than purely economic charts. He writes that he wanted to know: “what they were saying to one another, what the motivations were, what the incentives were.” 

The book underlines how credit and leverage were central in the boom years (banks' lending to speculators, margin purchases) and how many of the bank/industry titans either enabled or actively promoted that.

The narrative links the bubble not just to wild speculation but to structural features: the weak regulatory state, the interlocking roles of industry/finance/politics, banking’s dominance, and the illusion that “this time is different.” 

What emerges are critical banking reforms:

1. Forced separation in the banking industry between commercial lending arm and investment arm
2, Establishment of the FDIC to form a gov't backstop for banks and protect consumer confidence and present "runs on the bank"
3. Strengthening of the SEC and Federal Reserve

Parallels to 2025 and AI bubble? I really did not see much there!

The book goes into great detail about specific characters in the: 

A. Hoover Administration & Government Players

1. Herbert Hoover — President of the United States
Presided over the economy during the crash, initially minimizing the collapse and relying on voluntary cooperation rather than aggressive federal action.

2. Andrew W. Mellon — Secretary of the Treasury
Powerful financier-turned-Treasury Secretary whose laissez-faire, anti-intervention philosophy shaped the government’s restrained early response to the crash.

3. Carter Glass — U.S. Senator (later architect of GlassâSteagall)
One of the few political voices warning about speculative excess, representing the push for tougher regulation against dominant banks.

4. Roy A. Young — Chairman of the Federal Reserve Board
The cautious Fed leader who struggled to rein in speculation and faced open defiance from major banks when trying to tighten margin lending.

5. Eugene Meyer — Governor of the Federal Reserve Board (and later Fed Chairman)
Key internal Fed figure who argued for stronger action but faced political and institutional resistance.

B. Major Bankers & Wall Street Titans

6. Charles E. Mitchell — Head of National City Bank (Citigroup predecessor)
Perhaps the book’s greatest villain: aggressively fueled margin lending, openly undermined the Fed, and helped inflate the bubble.

7. Thomas W. Lamont — Senior Partner, J.P. Morgan & Co.
A central character whose diaries form a foundation of the book; attempted to coordinate rescues on Black Thursday but ultimately could not stop the collapse.

8. Albert Wiggin — Chairman of Chase National Bank
A powerful banker later revealed to have shorted his own bank’s stock during the crash, embodying conflicts of interest and insider manipulation.

9. Ben Smith & William Durant — Ad-hoc “market stabilizers”
Two wealthy figures who tried to prop up the market after the initial crash by buying up shares, illustrating the fragile efforts to restore confidence.

10. Richard Whitney — Vice President of the NYSE
Famous for his dramatic purchase of U.S. Steel shares on Black Thursday to halt panic selling, later disgraced for embezzlement.

C. Industry Titans, Corporate Figures & Speculative Actors
11. John J. Raskob — DuPont/GM executive; Democratic Party power broker
A symbol of 1920s optimism who encouraged ordinary Americans to buy stocks and used his corporate/political power to promote the bull-market ethos.

12. Jesse Livermore — Legendary speculator
The era’s most famous trader, who initially profited by shorting the market but became a tragic emblem of emotional and financial overreach.

13. William C. Durant — Founder of General Motors; serial market gambler
A wildly charismatic industrialist whose attempts to corner stocks exemplified the era’s reckless belief that the boom could be controlled by a few strong hands.

14. Arthur Wiesenberger — Market analyst and promoter
One of the public voices fanning retail investor enthusiasms, reflecting how media and newsletters contributed to speculative fever.

15. Evangeline Adams — Celebrity astrologer who advised investors

title: The Golden Road
author: William Dalrymple
notes:
I just listened to The Golden Road (William Dalrymple) on Spotify as a "free" audiobook, which allows 15 hours per month for books (this book was about 16 hours?). The print version has many historical maps and color photos, which would have been quite helpful (the book is on back order).

I found the book to be a gripping story told by an ardent storyteller who also is a researcher. The narrative takes a perspective that is little known in the West.

Dalrymple’s central claim is that, between roughly 250 BCE and ~1200 CE (or somewhat later), the Indian subcontinent was the fulcrum of a vast civilizational and economic sphere—a “Golden Road” of ideas, goods, and influences—spreading out across Eurasia, from the Roman world in the west to China, Korea, and Japan in the east. He argues that Indian learning, culture, religion (especially Buddhism and Hinduism), mathematics, science, art, architecture and trade had a much larger and earlier global impact than is often acknowledged. 

In his words (paraphrased): India was not just a passive recipient of external influences, but an active generator and exporter of culture and knowledge, connected through maritime and overland networks (monsoon-winds, maritime trade) that knit together a vast “Indosphere”. 

Here are the key supporting arguments and themes:

Maritime trade and the “Golden Road”

Dalrymple emphasizes how India’s geographical position, aided by monsoon winds, gave it access to maritime trade routes across the Indian Ocean, Red Sea, and beyond. 

He argues that this maritime trade preceded, and in many ways superseded, the overland “Silk Road” routes (which tend to dominate popular imagination). 

Example: trade from India into Roman Egypt and the Roman empire, bringing pepper, textiles, gemstones, luxury goods; the Roman writer Pliny called India “the sink of the world’s most precious metals”. 

The “Indosphere” and cultural influence

Dalrymple coins or uses the term “Indosphere” to describe the cultural-geographical zone influenced by India’s ideas, religions and languages (especially Sanskrit, Indian art/architecture, Buddhism, Hinduism) stretching across South Asia into Southeast Asia, East Asia and beyond. 

He highlights the spread of Buddhism from India into China, Korea, Japan; the adoption of Indian/Hindu cultural forms in Southeast Asia (temples, scripts, art) such as at Angkor Wat (Cambodia) or Borobudur (Indonesia). 

He emphasizes that many of these influences were non-coercive: the spread was by trade, pilgrimage, ideas — “soft power” — rather than by large-scale military conquest. 

Science, mathematics, knowledge transmission

Dalrymple argues that India made major contributions to mathematics (zero, the decimal system, algebra, trigonometry), astronomy (earth’s rotation, planetary motion) and that these ideas travelled from India to the Islamic world and then to Europe. 

For instance, he mentions the Indian mathematician Aryabhata and Brahmagupta, and the transmission of Indian numerals via the Abbasid world to the West (via figures like Fibonacci) in later centuries. 

Decline and transition

He argues that this period of Indian centrality eventually declines due to changing geopolitical and trade conditions: e.g., the arrival of Persianized Turkic empires, disruption of trade routes, the rise of Chinese and Central Asian power, and eventually the dominance of other networks. 

He also suggests that the reason this “Golden Road” narrative is under-emphasized in standard histories is due to biases (colonial historiography, Western-centric narratives, focus on Europe/China rather than India’s outward influence). 
History Reclaimed

Modern relevance

Dalrymple uses this history to reflect on how the past might inform present-day India and global dynamics: e.g., the idea of interconnectedness, soft power, cultural flows, and how India might reclaim or rediscover aspects of this legacy.

title: The Screwtape Letters
author: C. S. Lewis
notes:
I just re-read CS Lewis' Screwtape Letters!  I find this book to be so creative and hilarious (putting the deeper themes aside!).  This has kindled some interesting ideas for a project (more to follow).

The central thesis of The Screwtape Letters is that human beings are constantly subject to spiritual warfare, where subtle temptations and distractions orchestrated by demonic forces can lead them away from faith, virtue, and a relationship with God. 

The Screwtape Letters is structured as a series of 31 letters written by Screwtape, a senior demon, to his nephew Wormwood, a junior tempter. The epistolary format provides a one-sided correspondence, with each letter offering advice on how Wormwood should manipulate his human “patient” to secure his damnation. The letters are arranged chronologically, following the patient’s spiritual journey through various life events, such as falling in love, experiencing wartime anxiety, and grappling with faith.

One can contextualize other topics on similar grounds?

Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast, Ireland, in 1898 to a family of avid readers. Lewis, too, was soon immersed in literature: He started reading at just 3 years old, and by age 5, he had begun writing stories about a fantasy land populated by “dressed animals.”

 
Years later, a 19-year-old Lewis served in World War I with the Somerset Light Infantry. He experienced trench warfare on the front line in the Somme, the horrors of which he carried with him for the rest of his life.
Lewis first met J.R.R. Tolkien in 1926, and the two men developed a lifelong friendship. Lewis, who had become an atheist early in life, found his way back to theism and Christianity under Tolkien’s guidance. Tolkien, meanwhile, openly credited Lewis as a major source of creative encouragement: “Only from him,” wrote Tolkien, “did I ever get the idea that my âstuff’ could be more than a private hobby. But for his interest and unceasing eagerness for more I should never have brought The Lord of the Rings to a conclusion.”
Lewis himself was a prolific writer of both fiction and nonfiction. The latter included books and essays of Christian apologetics in which he passionately promotes and defends Christianity. Christian themes are also highly prevalent in his works of popular fiction, which include The Screwtape Letters, The Space Trilogy, and, most famously, The Chronicles of Narnia.
Here are 18 quotes from C.S. Lewis’ letters, essays, and literary works, covering a range of subjects from reading and writing to the importance of friendship.
Friendship is the greatest of worldly goods. Certainly to me it is the chief happiness of life. If I had to give a piece of advice to a young man about a place to live, I think I should say, “sacrifice almost everything to live where you can be near your friends.”

title: The Age of AI: And Our Human Future
author: Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt & Daniel Huttenlocher
notes:
Just read the 2021 book, The Age of AI: And Our Human Future, by Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, and Daniel Huttenlocher.

The book is almost quaint (4 years in AI is a lifetime!), warning of potential dangers of AI and need for global governance. The world has changed in the past 4 years, where the US has a markedly different posture towards the rest of the world (trade, competition, military), with a move away from global institutions (i.e. withdrew from multiple international accords and governance bodies) and towards a more transactional bipolar (rather than multi-polar) relation to other countries. The more polarized climate is less conducive to a global AI consensus or a kumbaya moment!

Summary of the Book

The Age of AI: And Our Human Future (2021), authored by Henry Kissinger, Eric Schmidt, and Daniel Huttenlocher, explores the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on society, politics, and human identity. The book, spanning seven chapters, traces AI’s evolution from philosophical roots in Enlightenment thinking to modern advancements, such as AI surpassing human performance in chess and discovering new antibiotics. It highlights AI’s potential to revolutionize fields like medicine, agriculture, and warfare, predicting that by 2040, AI could be a million times more powerful than in 2021. The authors emphasize AI’s dual nature—offering immense benefits, such as climate change mitigation, while posing risks like misinformation, autonomous weapons, and surveillance. They advocate for international cooperation and a national AI commission to guide ethical development, urging society to align AI with human values to shape a beneficial future.

Critique

The Age of AI is a disappointingly shallow and self-serving manifesto that prioritizes the agendas of its elite authors over substantive solutions to AI’s existential challenges. Written by a former statesman, a tech titan, and an academic, the book reeks of establishment hubris, offering a veneer of intellectual gravitas while sidestepping the gritty realities of AI’s societal impact. Its core argument—that AI’s transformative power demands cautious governance and ethical alignment—sounds profound but collapses under scrutiny for its lack of actionable proposals and uncritical deference to technocratic control.

First, the book’s historical analogies, such as comparing AI’s rise to the Enlightenment or World War I, feel forced and overly academic, serving more to inflate the authors’ intellectual credentials than to illuminate AI’s unique challenges. These comparisons, like the detour into Kant’s philosophy, are padded distractions that obscure the absence of concrete policy recommendations. For instance, the authors vaguely call for “mutual restraint” among nations but fail to engage with pressing issues like the global push for a ban on lethal autonomous weapons, a position supported by AI researchers and the International Committee of the Red Cross. This omission betrays a lack of courage to tackle controversial but urgent specifics.

Second, the authors’ proposal for a national AI commission—conveniently composed of figures like themselves—smacks of self-aggrandizement. This suggestion, presented as a solution to AI’s risks, ignores the dangers of concentrating power in the hands of unaccountable elites from government, Big Tech, and academia. The irony is palpable: a book warning about Big Tech’s potential to undermine democracy simultaneously advocates for tech moguls like Schmidt to shape AI policy. This reeks of a conflict of interest, especially given Schmidt’s Google tenure, which profited from data-driven AI systems that the book itself critiques for enabling surveillance and misinformation.

Moreover, the book’s optimism about AI’s benefits—such as revolutionizing medicine or mitigating climate change—glosses over the socioeconomic disruptions already underway. It barely addresses how AI-driven automation threatens livelihoods or exacerbates inequality, issues that demand immediate attention over speculative musings about human consciousness. The authors’ fatalistic view that AI’s development is inevitable dismisses the possibility of grassroots resistance or alternative technological paths, reinforcing a narrative that serves corporate and geopolitical interests rather than humanity at large.

Finally, the book’s accessibility, while marketed as a strength, dilutes its depth. It reads like a policy brief for the uninformed, lacking the rigor to engage experts or the specificity to guide policymakers. Its philosophical detours and lack of focus—evident in the poorly received Chapter 4—undermine its credibility as a definitive guide. Far from being “masterful,” as some claim, The Age of AI is a missed opportunity, a book that raises valid concerns but offers little beyond platitudes and a troubling vision of elite control over a technology that affects us all.

title: The Nvidia Way
author: Tae Kim
notes:
Just read the small book by Tae Kim, The Nvidia Way: Jensen Huang and the Making of a Tech Giant. It is a detailed business history of Nvidia, chronicling its journey from a 1993 startup founded in a Denny’s in East San Jose to becoming one of the world’s most valuable companies by 2024. Drawing on over 100 interviews, including with co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, the book explores how Nvidia’s unique culture and Huang’s unorthodox leadership drove its success in graphics processing units (GPUs) and artificial intelligence (AI) chips. 

The journey is characterized by serendipity, near death experiences, deft positioning of its products from gaming to AI, and seamless integration with Sega, Intel, Microsoft, Apple, and others.

Nvidia is at the center of the AI revolution, certainly from a hardware perspective and is a key bargaining chip in the tariff war with China.  Jensen predicts that all legacy data centers, that use conventional CPUs will be converted over to using GPUs in the near term.  In addition to this book, also consider 2 recent books (reviewed in earlier posts): Chip War by Chris Miller and The Coming Wave by Mustafa Suleyman.

Key Points:

Founding and Early Struggles: Nvidia was founded by Jensen Huang, Curtis Priem, and Chris Malachowsky to create PC-focused graphics chips. Early products like the NV1 and NV2 flopped due to misjudging market needs, nearly bankrupting the company. These failures taught Nvidia to prioritize customer demands and market fit.
Jensen Huang’s Leadership: Huang, the longest-serving tech CEO, is central to Nvidia’s story. His intense work ethic (working late nights and weekends), hands-on approach, and vision for long-term innovation shaped Nvidia’s culture. 

Notable practices include:

Top 5 Emails: Employees regularly send direct updates to Huang, bypassing bureaucratic filters to ensure transparency.

Flat Structure: Huang manages over 60 direct reports, fostering collaboration and reducing hierarchy.

Relentless Drive: Huang’s resilience, forged through early hardships like immigration and manual labor jobs, instilled a culture of perseverance and excellence.

Cultural Pillars: Nvidia’s “Nvidia Way” emphasizes:
Innovation Over Short-Term Gains: Huang invested heavily in technologies like CUDA (introduced in 2006) and ray tracing, often years before they became profitable, defying Wall Street’s pressure for quick returns.

Customer Focus: Post-early failures, Nvidia prioritized understanding market needs, leading to the successful RIVA 128 chip and later GPU dominance.
Mission-Driven Workforce: Employees are motivated by Nvidia’s impact on fields like AI, robotics, and digital biology, with many staying for decades despite intense demands.

Pivotal Innovations:

GPU Development: Nvidia standardized GPUs, revolutionizing gaming and later data centers. The 1997 RIVA 128 marked a turning point.
CUDA and AI: Huang’s early bet on CUDA enabled parallel computing, positioning Nvidia as the backbone of the AI revolution. By 2012, Nvidia GPUs powered breakthroughs like ImageNet, and by 2024, Nvidia held a near-monopoly in AI chips.
Strategic Acquisitions: The 2019 Mellanox acquisition bolstered Nvidia’s data center capabilities, a key factor in its AI dominance.
Overcoming Adversity: Nvidia faced near-fatal setbacks, including the 2013 stock stagnation that attracted activist hedge fund Starboard Value. Huang’s focus on long-term strategy, like CUDA investment, helped Nvidia outmaneuver rivals like Intel and avoid the “Innovator’s Dilemma.”

Market Impact: Nvidia’s stock grew at a 33% compound annual rate from its 1999 IPO to 2023, turning a $10,000 investment into $13.2 million. By June 2024, Nvidia briefly became the world’s most valuable company, driven by insatiable demand for its AI chips.

Themes and Takeaways:

Long-Term Vision: Huang’s ability to foresee markets (gaming, AI, data centers) and invest decades ahead set Nvidia apart.
Resilience: Early failures and Huang’s personal hardships shaped a culture that thrives on adversity.
Leadership Lessons: The book serves as both a thrilling history and a manual for entrepreneurs, highlighting Huang’s aggressive, customer-centric, and innovation-driven approach.
Societal Impact: Nvidia’s AI advancements are reshaping industries, from biomedicine to robotics, making it a cornerstone of the digital age.

Critiques:
Some readers note the narrative can feel uneven, with the first half being a slower, fact-heavy chronicle and the second half more engaging and novelistic.
The book skips some details, like Nvidia’s crypto boom or failed ARM acquisition, and occasionally overemphasizes technical chip details over broader analysis.

Reception:
The book is widely praised for its detailed storytelling, technical clarity, and insights into Huang’s leadership. It’s recommended for tech enthusiasts, entrepreneurs, and business leaders, though some find its focus on employee interviews slightly detracts from Huang’s personal story.

In summary, The Nvidia Way is a compelling account of Nvidia’s rise, driven by Huang’s visionary leadership and a culture of relentless innovation. It offers enduring lessons on resilience, long-term strategy, and building a market-leading company.  What is really interesting is that Jensen, at age 61, remains the longest serving founder / CEO of a major tech company and his identity is totally wrapped up in the DNA of the company. AI is at a pivotal point; there are many credible competitors so how Nvidia will adapt to succession planning is wholly unknown (to me anyway and the book does not really address this).

title: Abundance
author: Ezra Klein & Derek Thompson
notes:
Just read Abundance, co-authored by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson and published in March 2025 by Avid Reader Press. Book is only 226 pages, but I read it like a love letter (highlighted, underlined, with notes in the margins, etc.) and marinated in it! 

Book is well researched and referenced and it reviews recent American political movements, from the New Deal Liberalism of the 1930s (championed by FDR initially but also continued by Eisenhower a Republican), followed by the Neoliberal political order late 1970s (promulgated by Reagan’s individualism and continued by Bill Clinton, a free market democrat). A political movement or order is where there is a consensus of values and an approach embraced by both parties. Authors intimate that there may be an opening for a new political movement. 

The book’s first part is a critique of liberal governance in blue cities, with housing shortage, affordability crisis, homelessness, NIBYism, zoning laws, environmental regulations gone amok. Authors make the point that the solutions to a prior era (of excess industrialization and growth from the New Deal) resulted in a backlash to contain growth and preserve the environment, in fact championed under Nixon Republican governance (the clean air and water acts, EPA, etc.). That resulted in layers of bureaucracy which have lasted for decades.  There was extensive discussion of the critical role of government spending in jumpstarting major research efforts from OSRD (Office of Scientific Research and Development), NSF (National Science Foundation), and NIH (National Institutes of Health), leading to many technological miracles that we now take for granted. 

There was extensive discussion of the link between initial discovery or invention to practical implementation and scaling up to solve problems. Technologies were invented in America but built and mass produced in SE Asia, and we have lost the skill to make things. Reference was made to Wright’s Law, where innovation is enmeshed with the act of making, and goods become cheaper at scale (i.e. penicillin, Model T cars, solar panels, Covid period and Operation Warp Speed led to developing a new vaccine, organized by the government with incentives for the private sector where $40B was spent, free shots for the public, saved 20M excess deaths and perhaps $6T revenues all within 8 months. This massive effort could not have been made by any single entity and is an example of what can be done with focus. Interestingly, both parties stayed away from taking credit for this accomplishment (i.e. Trump did not run on this record!).

The authors offer a lens to view the world in terms of “scarcity” vs. “abundance.” They indicate that the political right has embraced scarcity as a baseline, and populists like Trump have taken politics to blame entities (immigrants, China) to forge a populist agenda. Alternatively,  you could consider an abundance agenda that liberalism might embrace for the future. 

The thesis is to identify certain existential problems such as the need for decarbonization for climate change, housing and affordability crisis, shortage of clean energy with the explosion of data centers and artificial intelligence as examples that could be focused on using technology and innovation, intentional planning with good governance, and cooperation. This will not be easy; it will require legislative changes at both the local level (YIMBYism) as well as the federal level.

They emphasize the “supply side” economic progressivism with new alliances with a goal of increasing production (in areas such as energy, housing) with technology at the heart of progress. Abundance is liberalism that builds. They view this as a political movement or order that can be an animating force that should be pursued. 

In summary, this was an outstanding read (was written largely prior to the election of Trump 2.0), with a nice mix of recent history, technology, and contemporary challenges. Authors clearly have a liberal pedigree, and I suspect this could be a blueprint for an aspiring national candidate!

I found the book to be uplifting, techno-optimistic, and forward looking. In my mind, they shifted the discussion away from left vs. right or big vs. small government, but more in the framework of scarcity vs. abundance paradigm. 
 
Unfortunately, much has happened in the country within weeks of publication of this book.

title: Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
author: Yuval Noah Harari
notes:
Just finished Yuval Noah Harari's 2024 book, "Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI". The book examines how humans have historically used information networks to cooperate, gain power, and shape societies. It also explores the challenges posed by the rise of artificial intelligence and the spread of misinformation.
The book was dense, full of references to history and how information networks evolved and were utilized. Harari, dating back to his earlier book Homo Sapiens, is a strong believer in the concept of stories, narratives, and myths as organizing principles in human history (that separate us from the other great apes). 

Key Themes:

1. Evolution of Information Networks: Harari traces the development of communication systems from early human societies (i.e. oral history, hand written church texts, printing press and printed bibles) to today's AI-driven networks, emphasizing how shared beliefs (even myths) have united large groups and enabled cooperation.

2. Dual Nature of Information: Information can serve both constructive and destructive purposes. The book highlights the complexity of distinguishing truth from fiction, especially in an era of AI-augmented narratives.

3. AI’s Role and Risks: Harari warns that AI, with intelligence untethered from human consciousness, poses existential risks. While AI can enhance efficiency and connectivity, it also raises concerns about manipulation, inequality, and the potential loss of human autonomy.

4. Human Agency in the AI Era: Harari stresses the urgency of making ethical and informed decisions about AI governance, arguing that these choices will determine humanity's future in the face of transformative technological change.

5. Historical Parallels: Through examples like witch hunts, totalitarian regimes, and modern populism, Harari illustrates how information networks have shaped societal dynamics and highlights the dangers of centralized information control.

"Nexus" serves as both a historical analysis and a cautionary tale, urging society to navigate the intersection of technology, information, and power thoughtfully. It highlights the potential for AI to either deepen cooperation or exacerbate societal divides depending on its use.

The book was highly informative about history, less so about current AI technology or specific winners or losers. He emphasizes "self-correcting networks" as a key factor separating benevolent forces from those that are not and prone to destruction (i.e. Hitler's world view). There are references to our current political state as well as a future of bot-on-bot world!  The second half of book was more relevant to current affairs. Also, there was a preachy tone and finger wagging in certain sections!

title: Age of Revolutions
author: Fareed Zakaria
notes:
I just read this excellent book (Age of Revolutions, Fareed Zakaria), which coincided with our national elections. Sometimes we get lost in the current day politics, but it helps to consider a longer-term perspective. In Part 1, Zakaria contextualizes 5 major past revolutions shaping the western world: Liberal revolution of the Netherlands, the Glorious (blood-less) revolution extending to England, the failed French revolution, the Industrial revolution in Britain as well as the parallel one in the US. He compares and contrasts these revolutions from the standpoint of liberalism vs. control by a king or the church. In Part 2, Zakaria posits there are 4 major current revolutions shaping the modern world: globalization (economics), information overload (technology), identitarian (tribal), and geopolitics. 

I found the discussion extremely educational as he frequently quotes from well-known thinkers; the section on American history itself was incisive. He takes vague references to more concretely discuss in detail (i.e. China Shock, Bretton Woods and the Washington Concensus, New Deal vs. neoliberal order, gunboat diplomacy, role of Luddites, Tocqueville, 5 stages of Vernon, etc.).  Of course, there was a lot of name-dropping for further study!  The timing of this book presages the contentious 2024 US election, and the unique role Trump is playing in scrambling current day politics.  

Zakaria is a current scholar & historian who takes a pragmatic approach to the world order.  I find him to be a sober thinker, especially as it pertains to the role of America in the current world order.

title: James
author: Percival Everett
notes:
Just read Percival Everett's latest book (James: A Novel), after watching his earlier book "Erasure" adapted into the Oscar nominated film American Fiction. James is a fictional re-telling of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (Twain's seminal work from the 1880s), but from the perspective of Jim (or James in Everett's version), the adult slave friend of Huck the teen! James is re-cast as an educated, scholarly man acutely aware of the hypocrisy living and "passing" in the stereotyped era, rather than just as a kindly but simple and superstitious slave man. 
I found James to be riotously funny, a clever perspective, providing an irreverant look into the absurdity of human bondage (and religion, social mores, etc). Any future high school English curriculum of necessity should assign James as an accompaniment to Huck Finn! Everett pays homage to Twain's vernacular and the story largely tracks with the original till a critical juncture!
This is a quick read and I would highly recommend it for any age reader. I suspect it will be the basis for a future Hollywood film?  The original Huck was banned in many places, so in our hyper-partisan era book-banning may still occur with James?
Best book I have read in many years!

title: How to Know a Person
author: David Brooks
notes:
Just read David Brooks' "How to Know a Person," and I will attempt a brief review (mostly to memorialize my thoughts, perhaps others might find value). David is of course a noted columnist for the NYT who has a "conservative" world view on politics. He has been on a personal journey to become a humanist, as he detailed in an earlier book (The Second Mountain) and even more publicly in this one! His journey has resonated with me (more than his politics?). This book is based on his research tapping into noted authors, many interviews with psychologists. The book borders between being "therapy" and a self-help guidance to be a better conversationalist, to be more empathic, to be better at responding to trials and tribulations in others.  The book has some practical information with multiple lists for asking the right questions, the Big 5 personality traits, practices to develop empathy, discussion of "life tasks" to work through or accomplish, to become an "illuminator" rather than a "diminisher" or a "topper." David quotes widely from history and literature and offers many individual stories that makes the book quite educational and fun.  I found chapter 10 (friend who is in despair) to be a good discussion of depression; the section on "life tasks" to be a thoughtful exposition of stages of life most of us complete with varied success; or the chapter on the 5 personality traits.
There were sections that were quite preachy with a darker world view, somehow things are much worse now than in years past. For example, under the section "epidemic of blindness", he discusses "moral formation" and abandonment in American institutions since WW-2, sounding much like the MAGA-movement for the wistful good old days ("can't stay away from them politics"!). Some of us may prefer the America of today than the 1930s-40s-50s for many reasons (was an era pre-medicare, SS, civil rights, etc). Every use of the word "morality" in the book made me recoil!
In summary, I do recommend this book as a strong read, as we are all on a journey to be better at being human, to support each other, at being better listeners, etc! There are many tangible tools offered.

title: Elon Musk
author: Walter Isaacson
notes:
Just read Walter Isaacson's biography on Elon Musk.  Isaacson is a brilliant biographer (I previously read books on Jen Doudna and Crisper/gene editing as well as one on Steve Jobs); as a biographer, he is not a "fanboy" nor a Musk hater, but paints Elon as a complex and polarizing figure, a transformative genius with major character flaws.  Musk, who is only 52, has humble origins in South Africa with an abusive father, comes to the US (via Canada), then transfers to Univ of Penn and subsequently ends up in Palo Alto to become a serial entrepreneur. 

At heart, he is a physics/math nerd, a video gamer, a steely risk taker with high functioning Asperger syndrome (low empathy, high IQ). He had outsized visions for humanity from early on (i.e. to go to Mars to preserve humanity, sustainable energy on earth, etc); an indomitable will to distort reality and make things happen. He was a control freak, didn't suffer fools, didn't care about others or their feelings per se. He thrived in high drama, adrenaline-junkie, etc  There were near-death experiences for all his corporate ventures.  

His first venture was Zip2 in the early 90s, a humble software (with map locations crossed with a business directory), then PayPal (bought by eBay). The subsequent and unlikely success of SpaceX (which created a reusable rocket to power astronauts to orbit as well as an orbiting satellite system Starlink to provide internet back on earth), then Tesla (largest maker of electric vehicles), and other ventures (SolarCity, Boring, Neuralink, Optimus). Of course, the infamous recent purchase of Twitter, the sewer of public human discourse. As distracting and obtuse as the purchase of twitter might be, access to massive datasets (500M tweets/day) together with Tesla video feeds from Autonomous cars could represent a rich “training” source for an improved AI platform (X.AI).  

The biography carefully dissects his personal life, his multiple wives, partners, and many children, extended family of cousins, etc. The book paints a picture of lack of impulse control, a desire to be in the limelight, to be in control, "rules don't apply to me", a god-complex.  The many houses, private jet travel, parties into the early morning hours, and work till you drop. The book also explores Musk's political transformation from being Obama-supporting liberal dude, to a libertarian to self-serving obsession with free speech (especially with Twitter) to embracing right wing conspiracy theories.  Sometimes blurring what is a joke, what is being a provocateur, to what is being hateful and abusive, to being of personal benefit!  Remember, the dude is only 52, is the richest man on the planet, he is touching and driving critical and transformative areas (space travel with contracts with NASA, car production (with innovative industrial design fabs, battery facilities, active attempts at full self-driving), de facto charging standard and network, energy, emerging AI competitor to ChatGPT). 

What is fascinating is that Musk has one foot in software/computers but the other foot on physical, industrial objects that moves matter!  In that way, he is of a different breed than many other tech titans!  I wouldn't want to be married or work for the dude or be his competitor!  This is a must read biography, consider it volume 1 only as the story is unfolding in front of our eyes!

title: Best Things First
author: Bjørn Lomborg
notes:
Just read the most eye-opening book by Bjorn Lomborg.  He proposes that the poorer half of the world (low income and lower-middle income countries) can be dramatically benefitted by a series of 12 specific measures that are highly cost-effective with remarkable benefit within a short time.  He uses concepts of "benefit-cost-analysis" and "discounting" and identifies measures wherein $1 invested must return atleast $15 or more in benefits. The academic analysis indicates that in aggregate investing $35B annually between 2023 and 2030 will save 4.5M lives each year and generate $1.1 trillion in other benefit per year! The interventions can be broken down into medical/public health (i.e malaria, TB, maternal health, childhood immunizations, nutrition, chronic disease) and all other (i.e. education, agriculture R&D, e-procurement, skilled migration, and land tenure).  As to who should/could fund this (i.e. from local gov'ts, rich countries, or private philantropy).  Interestingly, he argues against certain interventions as not being cost-effective (i.e. climate policies, clean drinking water/sanitation, and peace-keeping forces)!  
The bottom-line: this is a sound analysis and is the blueprint we should follow, if we take emotion out of the picture and be ruthlessly efficient!

https://www.amazon.com/Best-Things-First-Bjorn-Lomborg/dp/1940003482/ref=sr_1_1?crid=2IQGXSY7Q0HW3&keywords=bjorn+lomborg+best+things+first&qid=1690821902&sprefix=lomborg+best%2Caps%2C410&sr=8-1

title: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
author: Yuval Noah Harari
notes:
I am reading this incredible book (non-fiction) Sapiens, A History of Humankind (by Yuval Harari); I am only part way through it but had to share this with friends! The book is a non-technical account that spans the major developments in our species from hunter gatherer (over the cognitive, agricultural, and scientific movements) and separates biology and evolution from the uniquely human story telling/imagination as an organizing principle to organize millions of people; describes the man-made concepts of money, law, religion, math as a paradigm that is collectively subcribed by humanity.....simply brilliant! Will post more as I progress, no doubt!

notes:

title: The Wright Brothers
author: David McCullough
notes:
Just read David McCullough's The Wright Brothers; remains the most inspiring "story", to me somehow more captivating than most other human inventions; the sheer dogged persistence, physical skill and personal risk with a doubting world; all came to fruition in a relatively short period (about 5-10 years) that has changed history; the brothers had their flaws but for the most part were brilliant.  The book is a quick and easy read and is balanced between the aviation experiments as well as the deep bond between the siblings, sister, and father. I read the other book by Tom Couch, The Bishop's Boys about 30 years ago, which is deeper, etc. This deepens my current fixation with flying....

title: Democrats and Dissenters
author: Ramachandra Guha
notes:
Not sure this is an ideal place to post this since it might have limited general interest; but is a way for me to easily record my current thoughts.
I just finished a book titled Democrats and Dissenters (by Ramachandra Guha); https://www.amazon.com/Democrats-Dissenters-Ramachandra-Guha/dp/0670089362
Fabulous book for anyone with more than a casual interest in Indian political thought, written in 2016; Guha is truly a social scientist/scholar based in Bengaluru. He dispassionately discusses the pre-eminent scholars that influenced the independence movement and the post-colonial era. The writing style is easily understandable and allows the reader to become familiar with thought leaders from economics, political and social sciences. He is keenly aware of the current political dynamic and ascendency of hindu nationalism at both the local and national level (with the election of Modi and BJP). His final chapter titled "Where are the conservative intellectuals in India?" is a balanced indictment; and explores that inclusivity and broad-minded intellectual honesty is the only way forward for a multi-plural society.

title: The Code Breaker
author: Walter Isaacson
notes:
Just read (a la heard as an audio book)  Walter Isaccson's Code Breakers (https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/The-Code-Breaker/Walter-Isaacson/9781982115852);
Is an exceptional "biography" about Jeniffer Duda, a chemist/geneticist who is credited with co-developing CRISPR (was awarded the Nobel prize recently). The story is riveting, the science is complex but brilliant. Isaccson humanizes the science, the competitive forces, etc to make it a great read. I suggest "listening" to this book more than reading it since some of the detail is really complex and probably not worth getting bogged down in. But the CAS-9, concept of simply editing RNA, uses in both somatic cells (non-heritable) and germline  cells (inheritable), etc was made easier for a non-scientist to grasp. This technology (obviously a collective human effort by many labs around the world) is revolutionizing our approach to many intractable disorders (e.g. sickle cell, CF, retinal, etc). Mostly, it is a "simple tool". There was much discussion on the ethics, etc and some "semonizing"......overall, excellent.
